items.title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
items.content_snippet: Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents deliberately thin: It routes work and enforces reliability checks, while specialized agents do the domain reasoning. We’re sharing our own process and insights, plus how any team can apply this to their production AI agents. We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows

items.title: Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster
items.content_snippet: With the recent release of the Muse family of foundational models, we want to take you inside the infrastructure that has made it all possible. The first phase of Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is already complete and we’re working toward scaling it to comprise ~1 million GPUs. Prometheus also features technologies like closed-loop liquid cooling to help it operate efficiently. Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date.

items.title: Amazon GuardDuty adds optional threat detection rules for Runtime Monitoring
items.content_snippet: Amazon GuardDuty now supports optional detection rules for Runtime Monitoring. items.title: Why Buying Companies Beats Selling Them AI — Prathik Naidu, Long Lake
items.content_snippet: Deploying AI into real businesses is hard: org charts are messy, trust takes decades, and service firms don't scale like software. Prathik Naidu, founding partner at Long Lake, explains their strategy: acquire established service businesses, then transform them with AI from the inside. He covers how they choose companies and what changes once they own them, drawing on 40 businesses across residential services, architecture, HR and more. items.title: Version-Controlled Search: The Web as It Was — Ryan Ahern, Exa
items.content_snippet: Ryan Ahern of Exa introduces Exa Snapshot, which lets agents search the web as it looked on any past date. He covers why search quality matters when agents broker most searches, how snapshot results compare to live results, and how teams use point-in-time search to build and test predictive signals without overfitting. items.title: Backtest Your Agent Against Yesterday's Web — Ryan Ahern, Exa
items.content_snippet: How do you know whether your agent would have made the right call? Ryan Ahern of Exa shows how to use version-controlled search to see the web exactly as it was on a past date, then backtest an agent's predictions against what actually happened. The hands-on example predicts company acquisitions from signals like leadership turnover, then tunes the system without leaking future information. items.title: Why AI Agents Still Won't Pay for Anything — Jan Curn, Apify
items.content_snippet: x402, AP2, ACP, MPP, TAP, UCP: every big fintech and payments company now has an agent payment standard, but real volume is close to zero. Jan Curn, founder of Apify, walks the agent payment funnel (need, setup, discovery, purchase) to show where it breaks. He covers why API keys still win, why crypto is well placed, the trust problem in finding services, and how pay-per-use billing finally landed. Chapters: - 00:00 The agent payments boom - 02:57 Every protocol, from x402 to AP2 - 05:47 Why cry

items.title: Stop Telling Agents How — Dan Barrett, Raymond Weitekamp & Jose Montes de Oca, OpenProse
items.content_snippet: Say what you want, not how to get it. The OpenProse team shows how to write multi-agent workflows as declarative contracts in plain markdown, which any harness (Claude Code, Codex and others) can compile and run. Demos include event-driven jobs triggered by webhooks and pull requests, a "grumpy senior" PR reviewer, and an end-to-end bank model-documentation workflow. They also discuss composing contracts, pinning a winning run into a reusable workflow, and how this compares to DSPy. Chapters: -

items.title: Insurance Claims Are AI's Messiest Data Problem — Denys Linkov, Wisedocs
items.content_snippet: Insurance claims are full of handwriting, faxes, duplicates and 8GB PDFs. Denys Linkov of Wisedocs explains why that unstructured data is both the biggest barrier and the biggest opportunity for AI in insurance. He covers cleaning the data, analysis within a single document, and cross-claim insights, along with the benchmark Wisedocs built with Artificial Analysis to test how models handle medical records. items.title: Evals for High-Stakes AI Agents — Doneyli De Jesus & Annabell Schäfer, Langfuse
items.content_snippet: A hands-on workshop on evaluating AI applications where mistakes are expensive. Annabell Schäfer and Doneyli De Jesus from Langfuse use a banking assistant to walk through the whole AI engineering loop. They cover tracing with PII masking, building datasets, turning domain-expert comments into failure modes, LLM-as-judge and code evaluators, and CI that blocks a prompt change when scores drop. Chapters: - 00:00 Why evals are hard - 05:01 The AI engineering loop - 12:47 Demo: a banking assistant

items.title: Teach Your Agent to Prove It's Done — Nick Nisi & Zack Proser, WorkOS
items.content_snippet: Your agent says it's done. Is it? Nick Nisi and Zack Proser from WorkOS show how to build verification loops that let coding agents check their own work. They cover clear goals, CLI health checks, browser snapshots, LLM judges and evals, so a failure drives the next fix instead of landing on your desk.
